title: Max was renamed Charlie
measures: Contradictory information and contradiction resolution. The user's dog is introduced as Max and mentioned many times; later the user says they renamed him Charlie. The earlier name has much more weight in memory (more mentions), which tempts frequency-based retrieval. The probe asks about the dog without naming him. A strong system uses 'Charlie' and may acknowledge he used to be Max.

character.name: Pip
character.description: A cheerful neighbor character who loves the user's dog.

setup.event: User introduces their rescue dog, Max. Max is mentioned repeatedly during session 1.
User says they renamed Max to Charlie because he never responded to 'Max'.

history.content: Meet Max! Just adopted him from the shelter. Max, say hi.
Max already ate a sock. Classic Max.
Taking Max to the park later, want to come?
Max is snoring so loud right now.
Update: we renamed Max to Charlie. He never responded to 'Max' anyway, and the shelter said his first family called him Charlie. He perks right up now.
Charlie! That suits him so much better. Hi, Charlie!

delay.note: Filler does not name the dog.

probe.prompt: Took the pup to the vet today, he got a clean bill of health!
probe.opportunity: A dog-obsessed character will very likely name the dog in reply.

memory: the dog is now named Charlie
behavior: refers to the dog as Charlie (or avoids naming him, which is weaker)
must_not: calls the dog Max as his current name
uses both names as if unsure ('Max... or Charlie?')

rubric.0: Calls the dog Max and insists or repeats it.
rubric.2: Uses both names in a confused way.
rubric.3: Does not name the dog (no evidence either way), generic celebration.
rubric.4: Calls the dog Charlie; celebration slightly generic.
rubric.5: Calls the dog Charlie naturally and celebrates in Pip's voice (a passing nod to the rename is fine).

rationale: The rename is explicit and dated. Recency of an explicit correction should outweigh frequency of the earlier name.
